paragraphs: In the ninth month of the twenty-first year of Taiyuan, the night rain had chilled the tiles of the palace in Jiankang.

Beyond the palace walls, Zhu Xu emerged from the Censorate into a street emptied of passersby. His attendant carried a lantern; its wet paper clung to the bamboo ribs whenever the wind blew. In Zhu Xu’s sleeve lay a returned order for examining evidence. The seal of the Kuaiji regional office should have stood upon it. Instead there were four small characters: Await imperial review.

More than a year had passed since Lu Xiaoqi died on the imperial avenue. They had found the palace gate’s duty register for that night and obtained the carter’s testimony. But who had ordered the soldiers to drive off the petitioners? The officer on duty said he had received spoken instructions from his superior; the superior maintained that he had been at the banquet. Zhu Xu still held the handwritten order he had obtained from the inner palace. Yet whenever the inquiry required cross-checking land rolls, military registers, and palace guard records, it stopped.
“General, shall we go to the Eastern Residence?” the attendant asked.
“No.” Zhu Xu glanced at the palace city. “His Majesty may not sleep tonight.”
Sima Yao was indeed awake.

The silver candles in the inner hall had burned low. His wine cup sat beside the desk, but he was still reading dispatches from Jingzhou. Yin Zhongkan had commissioned more tower ships at Jiangling. Jingkou had not received its full allotment of grain and pay, while Jiankang wanted another contingent of imperial guards, ostensibly against both Jingzhou and Jingkou. Verification rolls for land taxes in the Three Wu commanderies lay in a heap. The estates of several powerful clans occupied even less land on paper than the year before, although villages in neighboring counties lay deserted and the collectors pressed harder for the regular tax.

Sima Yao held down the page with one finger and took up the agreement from the Huai submitted by Zhu Xu. The ruler of Qin offered three years without border hostilities, free exchange of goods, and no forcible return of refugees. The language was hardly deferential; every sentence left a way out. He had meant to summon Zhu Xu personally and ask whether Fu Jian feared another war or had made the North secure enough to wait at his leisure.
A young palace eunuch entered to inquire after him. Sima Yao asked, “Where are the Kuaiji land registers I requested the day before yesterday?”
“The Department of State Affairs reports that heavy rains have made the roads impassable. The records are still on their way.”
“They were said to be on their way last year.”
The eunuch bowed even lower.

Sima Yao waved him away. His wine was cold, but he drank it nonetheless. In youth he had imagined that one day he would reclaim affairs of state, piece by piece, from imperial kinsmen and the great houses. Only later had he discovered that every gate in the capital had its own keeper. If he used Jingkou’s troops to check Sima Daozi, Jingkou demanded provisions; if he relied on Sima Daozi to restrain Jingzhou, Jingzhou recruited men in the name of guarding the frontier. When he ordered an inquiry into aristocratic estates, regional offices sent him petitions from commoners while leaving the great families’ deeds locked away.
“Summon them tomorrow,” he told an attendant. “The Prince of Kuaiji and Liu Laozhi. If Zhu Xu has arrived, he is to bring the agreement into the palace.”
The attendant hesitated. “General Liu has no order to come to the capital, Your Majesty. He may not be able to—”
Sima Yao set down the cup.
“Must someone grant me leave before I can summon my own general?”
The man threw himself down, protesting that he had meant no such thing.

The night deepened, and the rain eased. Someone replaced the lampwicks beneath the eaves; someone brought fresh wine. Who remained at Sima Yao’s side afterward could never be established. One deposition said the emperor drank alone; another spoke of an argument; a third recorded only the hour when a pot of warmed wine had been delivered. Each bore a fingerprint, but none could account for the final hour.

Before dawn, a maid on night duty saw that the lamp in the inner hall was still burning, though no sound came from the imperial bed. She called twice through the curtain. Approaching, she saw overturned cups, wine spreading from the bed’s edge down to the footstool, and the emperor’s right hand hanging beyond the coverlet, its fingers still slightly curved as though around a cup.
The maid retreated to the doorway without crying out. She feared that if she called too soon, she would be named the last person to approach the bed.

After inspecting the scene, the palace chamberlain sealed the hall and summoned the physicians. One was pulled from his bed so hurriedly that he put on his headcloth crooked. Kneeling beside the emperor, he felt for a pulse, examined the face, pressed the chest, and at last withdrew his hands into his sleeves. Sima Daozi arrived with rain-mud on his boots.
“Well?”
The physician swallowed. “His Majesty had long been overburdened and had drunk heavily. By the time I arrived, his pulse and breath had stopped.”
“I asked for the cause of death.”
“All I can determine is a sudden death. Drink and his former ailment may both have contributed. If a closer examination is required—”
Sima Yuanxian stepped out from behind his father. “Where are the people who served the wine last night?”

The detained attendants knelt in a row. Each gave a different hour; those who brought the wine and those who cleared the cups denied seeing one another. Yuanxian ordered the guards to record every name and let no one leave the palace. Daozi stood just inside the doorway, looking at his brother on the bed, before saying, “Inform the crown prince’s residence first. Let the guards remain at their posts; no unauthorized changes. Seal all duty records.”
Yuanxian murmured, “Father, we must take control of the palace gates first.”
“Take control,” Daozi replied. “But do not let anyone write ‘By order of the Prince of Kuaiji’ on the gate notices.”

By the hour of the dragon, the palace gates were still shut. Officials assembled outside in a damp, confused knot. Some wore soaked court robes; others had been roused from their couches by servants and hurried in without knowing what had happened. Zhu Xu stood among them, holding the agreement between the two states wrapped in oilcloth. Before setting out, he had also taken the response to the Kuaiji land case, hoping the emperor might issue an unambiguous command. His steps slowed when he saw that the Prince of Kuaiji’s carriages were already inside.
Zhu Xu stood below the palace steps when the mourning bell began to toll.

After the first stroke, nobody dared ask. At the second, an elderly minister in the front rank sank to his knees. Only with the third did word come through the gates that the emperor was dead. Figures collapsed across the wet stone, and weeping rose in one place, then spread down the long galleries. Zhu Xu knelt erect, rainwater running from his forehead along his nose.

He remembered the morning Xiangyang fell. When the enemy breached the walls, at least he knew there were armed men outside and which gate he might defend. Today no enemy army stood before Jiankang, yet every palace gate had already been shut from within.

That afternoon the crown prince, Sima Dezong, ascended the throne. An official of rites presented the jade seal before the dais. The young emperor looked at it without reaching out. An attendant bent to his ear and repeated a few words, but he continued staring at a brick newly washed clean by rain. Sima Daozi stepped forward, took his hand, and helped him receive the seal. The officials prostrated themselves and cried, “Ten thousand years!” Their prolonged acclamation passed through the rain beyond the palace walls.

Zhu Xu stood in the last rank. In Chang’an he had seen the Department of State Affairs when Fu Jian fell ill: for every military order, someone had to produce credible authentication and identify who would execute it. They had argued until their faces reddened, but at least words spoken beside a sickbed could not pass for a promulgated edict. In Jiankang that day, no one dared ask whose hand would wield the new emperor’s seal or whose brush would write in his name.

Three orders were issued that evening. Frontier garrisons were to hold their own districts and not move troops without leave. Jingkou was to detach its finest soldiers to guard Jiankang and submit the remaining military rolls for review at the center. Private boats were forbidden to travel north at the Huai crossings, and all correspondence with Qin was to be sealed. The finance authorities also requested higher levies to pay for the state funeral and palace guard. Clerks receiving these documents found their details mutually contradictory, but none wished to be first to carry objections into the palace.

The Censorate’s Kuaiji land case was sealed as well. The files checked under lamplight the previous evening—Lu Fu’s lost fields, the cause of Lu Xiaoqi’s death, and the levies imposed on fugitive households—went into a different wooden box. A new label read: Unfinished business of the late emperor; await later deliberation.

Zhu Xu sought permission to inspect the records. The recording clerk avoided him. He waited in the corridor until dusk, when a young scribe slipped him a page of a damaged copy: one entry for the change of the palace guards on that night the previous year had been altered. No one knew where the original had gone.
“Who changed it?” Zhu Xu asked.
The scribe shook his head. “General, you must not tell anyone that I gave you this page today.”

Zhu Xu put away the fragment and went to the Eastern Residence the next day. The agreement between Qin and Jin was already in Sima Daozi’s possession, with a bronze animal-shaped paperweight on its edge.
“The ruler of Qin promises not to take up arms for three years?” Daozi asked.
“That is what his letter says.”
“And he will provide grain and receive those who flee south. How generous.”

“Refugees in Qin also contend over land,” Zhu Xu replied. “Relief grain must be raised; local officials seize the chance to take households for themselves. I have seen both the benefits and the abuses.”
Sima Yuanxian interjected, “You have examined matters so carefully that one might think you went to audit the government in Chang’an for them.”

Zhu Xu turned to the young heir. “I defended a Jin city. I was also a prisoner of Qin. If I can watch a country’s people starve and speak only of which dynasty holds the rightful succession, these eyes have been wasted all these years.”
Fury rose in Yuanxian’s face. Daozi put a hand on the agreement, preventing his son and the veteran general from quarreling openly.
“General Zhu, the southern court will never readily approve a treaty made on equal terms with Qin. Now we have a state funeral. Let the matter rest.”
“The late emperor intended to receive me himself.”
“The late emperor is dead.”

After those four words Zhu Xu had nothing more to say. Daozi glanced at his wooden box and added, “You investigated the Three Wu commanderies at his command. You may still testify at the Censorate about what you saw. But without a new edict, you may not requisition records from the prefectures or commanderies on your own authority.”

The files went back to the archive under seal; the keys, however, passed into the hands of the accused man’s confidants. Zhu Xu left the Eastern Residence and fastened the oilcloth beneath the stone steps. The wooden box was empty now, but the damaged copy remained in his sleeve.

News from Jiankang reached Jingkou as Liu Laozhi was inspecting bows on the drill ground. A courier presented three edicts. Liu read them one by one and laid them in a row upon his desk: defend Jingkou; send five thousand men to guard the capital; forward the troop registers to Jiankang. Each order had to be obeyed; taken together, they made it impossible to tell which to carry out first.
An adviser asked, “General, from which camp shall we draw the palace guard?”
Liu Laozhi answered with a question: “If stripping Jingkou of troops leaves it exposed, whom will the court blame for its fall?”

Some urged him to reject the edict. Others wanted to send troops into Jiankang first and seize the granaries; still others proposed secret correspondence with Jingzhou. Liu Laozhi tired of the talk, dismissed them all, and kept only Liu Yu behind.

Liu Yu had not yet risen high enough to sit among the generals as an equal. His uniform still bore the wear from the last grain inspection. He stood by the entrance, his eyes fixed on the edict concerning the military rolls.
“What is it you want to say now?” Liu Laozhi asked.
“I would ask about the grain first, General.”
“Are you the only man in Jingkou capable of asking about grain?”
“Five thousand men will eat on the road, and they will eat in Jiankang. Will the capital supply them properly for every man? If not, from whom will the soldiers demand food?”
Liu Laozhi gave a snort. He had expected Liu Yu to lecture him once more on the great duties of war and state. Instead he heard what everyone in camp was asking.
“And your next question?”
“Under whose command will they serve in the capital? If someone orders them to raid a minister’s residence, are they protecting the emperor or fighting another man’s quarrel?”
“The court has the imperial seal!”
“A prefect’s private order may bear a seal too,” Liu Yu said. “Two years ago, Jiang Shun’s family nearly got dragged back as deserters on the strength of a few stamped papers.”
Liu Laozhi stared at him. “You compare Jiang Shun’s case to an imperial edict?”
“I would not presume to judge the emperor, General. I only want to know who must speak plainly before the swords leave their scabbards.”

Footsteps crunched on gravel beyond the tent. Liu Laozhi paced to the window and stood there for some time. “Leave sufficient troops to defend Jingkou. Ask for ten days’ grace before sending the guard. The military rolls are under review; report the true numbers tomorrow. And do not make more trouble.”
Liu Yu assented but did not leave. Liu Laozhi looked back. “What else?”
“If you cannot keep your own word, General, whoever comes from the court or Jingzhou will use the Northern Garrison as a battering ram against the palace gates.”

Liu Laozhi raised a hand to rebuke him, then lowered it. When he first knew Xie Xuan, the Northern Garrison had been a blade of one piece. Now everyone who gripped its hilt watched to see which way it would fall. After Liu Yu left, Liu Laozhi placed the three edicts beneath a stone inkstone on his desk, as though a gust off the Yangtze might otherwise scatter them.

A letter arrived from Jingzhou too. Under cover of mourning, Yin Zhongkan asked whether Jingkou would join him in setting Jin’s house to rights. Liu Laozhi read it once and did not reply. The blank paper for his response lay untouched until midnight. The lamp oil ran out, and the sheet was still white.

Meanwhile, Zhu Xu passed through Jiankang’s western market. A paper shop stood half-shuttered. After the rain, the peddlers were peeling apart soaked sheets and spreading them to dry. Lu Fu lived in a lane behind the market. The old man’s back was more bent than a year before, and his grandson’s old shoe hung on the wall, dried hard and twisted out of shape. Zhu Xu told him the case files had been sealed and no one knew when the investigation could resume.
Lu Fu looked at him. “General, does the paper the late emperor gave you still count?”
For a long time Zhu Xu was silent. Then he spread the damaged copy, with its traces of alteration, under the lamp.
“The paper remains,” he said. “I know the writing on it.”
Lu Fu bent over it for a long while before asking only, “Is Xiaoqi’s name still there?”
“It is.”

The old man took down the stiff little shoe, threaded it again with cord, and hung it on its nail. Outside, the mourning bells in the palace city had ceased, but the rain had not. Zhu Xu picked up his lantern and walked out of the lane. More petitions from fugitive households would arrive from south of the Huai tomorrow. He did not know whether the new court would receive them. For now, he began thinking how to put a long bench under shelter from the rain outside the Censorate gate.
